summary:
Australia treats gender identity as a protected ground under the federal Sex Discrimination Act, in force since 2013. In August 2024 the Federal Court held in Tickle v Giggle that gender-identity discrimination protection extends to trans women as women, and awarded compensation against a female-only dating app that had excluded a trans woman member. The Commonwealth statute was amended by the Sex Discrimination Amendment (Sexual Orientation, Gender Identity and Intersex Status) Act 2013, prohibiting discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity and intersex status alongside sex, marital or relationship status, pregnancy and breastfeeding across work, accommodation, education and the provision of goods and services.

The external territories have no territory-specific SOGIE statute and no documented divergence from that national framework. Norfolk Island has been part of New South Wales legislation from 1 July 2016 under the Norfolk Island Legislation Amendment Act 2015 and the Territories Legislation Amendment Act 2016. Christmas Island and the Cocos (Keeling) Islands are jurisdictions where Western Australia laws apply. Jervis Bay Territory stands under the national layer, with no state-level instrument named in the sources. The Sex Discrimination Act applies throughout Australia including the external territories governed directly by Commonwealth law, so a visitor on Norfolk Island, Christmas Island, the Cocos (Keeling) Islands or Jervis Bay Territory is covered by that statute with no local provision narrowing it.

Availability of the 'X' sex descriptor and anti-discrimination protection on the grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity or expression extend across the states and territories with concurrent federal protection. Same-sex adult private sexual conduct has been legal nationally since the Human Rights (Sexual Conduct) Act 1994 commenced on 19 December 1994.

Visitors encounter none of the restrictive machinery found elsewhere: there are no laws confining bathrooms or changing facilities by gender identity, no border friction has been reported for trans travellers, and marriage equality has held since 2017, which matters to same-sex couples arriving together.
tangentialFactors:
State law has moved in the same direction as the federal statute. Queensland strengthened discrimination and vilification protections for gender-diverse people in April 2024 through its human rights commission's reform program, and New South Wales passed the Equality Legislation Amendment (LGBTIQA+) Act 2024. Those two instruments set the floor beneath which the New South Wales and Western Australia laws applying to Norfolk Island, Christmas Island and the Cocos (Keeling) Islands operate.

Counterweights are documented. The Tickle case itself grew out of organised exclusionary activism. ANROWS research maps current and emerging threats to trans and gender diverse rights in Australia, naming organised exclusionary campaigns, disputes over access to facilities and to records, and pressure to roll back existing rights.

No comparable national-level assessment of the four external territories was located, so the threat picture for Norfolk Island, Christmas Island, the Cocos (Keeling) Islands and Jervis Bay Territory rests on the national and state findings rather than on territory-specific evidence.
localsOnly:
Detention carries the sharpest residual risk for residents as well as visitors. Queensland's 2009 corrective services procedure on transgender prisoners was assessed as largely ineffective; oversight passed to the Inspector of Detention Services Act 2022, fully in force from 2023, and inspection standards issued in August 2023 for Queensland prisons and youth detention centres direct that transgender and intersex prisoners are generally admitted to facilities corresponding to their lived or experienced gender. Placement is therefore identity-based, with a discretionary admission caveat and an exception tied to sexual reassignment surgery.

Residents of Norfolk Island are covered by New South Wales equality and anti-discrimination law from 1 July 2016, and residents of Christmas Island and the Cocos (Keeling) Islands by Western Australia law, each with concurrent national protection on the same grounds.

ANROWS research documents systemic discrimination and harassment experienced by trans people across Australia, which describes the everyday environment residents of these units share with the mainland states.
outOfScopeNotes:
The state-level framework governing Jervis Bay Territory is not named in the sources available for this record; only its standing under the national layer is sourced. This is unresolved.

The Queensland Human Rights Commission announcement of better discrimination protections for gender-diverse people was not retrievable at its source URL (HTTP 403). The April 2024 reform is carried here from the source title and from a separate account of the same change, so the precise scope of the Queensland instrument is unresolved.

No territory-specific enforcement data, incident record, facility rule or complaint outcome was found for Norfolk Island, Christmas Island, the Cocos (Keeling) Islands or Jervis Bay Territory. Whether marker issuance and discrimination-complaint handling operate identically to the mainland processes on each unit is not separately sourced.
